name: Languages that compile to SQL
summary: Query languages such as Malloy, PRQL and Logica that a compiler turns into SQL, so you write in a cleaner syntax and the database you already have runs the result.
howItWorks: The language is only a front end. You write a query in its own syntax: a pipeline of steps (PRQL), a semantic model plus queries over it (Malloy, Looker’s LookML), logic rules (Logica), or method calls in a host language (LINQ in C#, Ibis in Python). A compiler parses that, resolves names against the tables or model, builds a relational plan and prints SQL for a target dialect, so the same query can come out with `LIMIT 10` for DuckDB and `OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY` for SQL Server. The database receives ordinary SQL and parses, optimizes and executes it as if a person had written it; the language adds no server, storage or engine of its own. Because a compiler is only as broad as what it can translate, most of these languages keep an escape hatch for raw SQL, such as PRQL’s `s"..."` strings or Malloy’s SQL sources. The opposite approach changes SQL itself: GoogleSQL’s pipe syntax lets a query read as a pipeline of `|>` steps inside SQL, with no separate compiler or new language to adopt.
analogy: Dictating to a stenographer. You speak in your own shorthand and the stenographer types up a formal letter. The person who receives it (the database) only ever sees the formal letter, so nothing changes on their side, but you never have to write one yourself.
useWhen: Analysts write long SQL with nested subqueries, repeated expressions and copy-pasted logic, and want variables, functions or pipelines instead
The same query has to run on several engines, such as DuckDB on a laptop and BigQuery or Snowflake in production
Business definitions (an on-time rate, net revenue) should live once in a model and be reused by every query
You want to read, review and test the SQL that actually runs, rather than trust an opaque tool
avoidWhen: Your team already writes good SQL and the engine supports what you need, including pipe syntax where it exists: another language is one more thing to learn and debug
Queries depend on engine-specific features the compiler doesn’t translate; you’ll fall back to raw SQL anyway
Writes and transactions: these languages are built for reading and transforming data, not for `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or DDL
Every tool in the chain (BI, notebooks, CI linting, the database console) would need to understand the new language
example: A product analyst’s weekly report is 200 lines of SQL: three nested subqueries, the same `CASE` expression pasted four times, and a `HAVING` clause nobody can explain. She rewrites it in PRQL as one pipeline: `from orders`, `filter`, `derive` the shared expression once, `group` by country with `aggregate`, then `filter` again on the totals. The compiler turns the first `filter` into `WHERE` and the second into `HAVING`, and prints SQL for the team’s DuckDB notebooks and for ClickHouse in production. The pull request includes both the PRQL and the generated SQL, so reviewers who only know SQL can still check what will run.

providers.aws: No compile-to-SQL language of its own. SQL produced by these compilers runs on Athena or Redshift like any hand-written query
providers.gcp: Looker, whose SQL generator compiles LookML models into SQL; BigQuery pipe syntax (`|>`) as the in-SQL alternative, on by default for all users since February 2025; Logica, an open-source language from Google engineers (not an official Google product)
providers.azure: No compile-to-SQL query language as a cloud service. In .NET, LINQ queries over `IQueryable` are translated to SQL by providers such as Entity Framework Core
providers.oss: Malloy (MIT), PRQL (Apache 2.0), Logica (Apache 2.0), Ibis (Python dataframes compiled to SQL), Apache Spark SQL pipe syntax (since Spark 4.0)

sections.title: Four ways to avoid writing SQL by hand
sections.intro: All of them end up as SQL; they differ in what you write instead.

items.name: Pipelines
items.text: A query is a list of steps, each transforming the result of the one before, read top to bottom. PRQL’s `filter` becomes `WHERE` or `HAVING` depending on where it sits. SaneQL, proposed at CIDR 2024, chains operators in the same way; its prototype translates to SQL.

items.name: Semantic models
items.text: Joins, dimensions and measures are defined once in a model, and queries refer to them by name. Malloy and Looker both generate the SQL, including the joins, from the model; Malloy can also nest one query’s results inside each row of another.

items.name: Logic programming
items.text: Queries are written as Datalog-style rules that can build on each other, and the compiler turns them into SQL. Logica, released by Google engineers in 2021 as the successor to Google’s Yedalog, targets BigQuery, PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB.

items.name: Host-language queries
items.text: The query is code in a general-purpose language. C#’s LINQ builds expression trees that providers such as Entity Framework Core translate to SQL; Ibis builds a lazy Python expression and compiles it to the SQL dialect of the chosen backend. This overlaps with ORMs.

sections.title: A new language, or pipes inside SQL?
sections.intro: Google’s pipe syntax paper argues that new languages haven’t displaced SQL because adopting them is costly, and adds pipelines to SQL itself instead.

rows.label: What you write
values: SQL, with `FROM` first and `|>` between steps

rows.label: Where it runs
values: Any database the compiler has a dialect for
Only engines that implement it: BigQuery and other GoogleSQL systems, Spark 4.0 and later

rows.label: Extra tooling
values: A compiler, plus editor and notebook support

rows.label: Beyond plain SQL
values: Variables, functions, reusable models, nested results
Clauses in any order, any number of times; existing queries keep working

story: SQL has had critics almost since it appeared, and many attempts to replace it never left the database they were built for. A different idea is to keep SQL as the format that databases receive and put a better language in front of it. Microsoft’s LINQ did this inside C#, with providers that translate queries to SQL. Looker’s LookML did it for business intelligence: analysts describe joins, dimensions and measures, and Looker’s SQL generator writes the queries. In April 2021 Google engineers Konstantin Tretyakov and Evgeny Skvortsov released Logica, a Datalog-like successor to Google’s Yedalog, arguing that SQL’s main flaw is its very limited support for abstraction.

The same year, Looker co-founder and LookML inventor Lloyd Tabb and a team at Google started Malloy, a modelling and query language that compiles to SQL and handles nested data; it reached its stable 4.0 version in October 2023 and is now a Linux Foundation (LF Projects) series. On 1 January 2022 Maximilian Roos made the first commit to PRQL, a pipelined language whose compiler is written in Rust. ClickHouse added PRQL as an experimental dialect in release 23.7 in 2023, and DuckDB gained a community extension for it. The GitHub list “Languages that compile to SQL” gathers these and others, from Ermine to Datalog converters.

In 2024 two papers took stock. At CIDR, Thomas Neumann and Viktor Leis of TU Munich analysed real queries (50,683 of those submitted to the HyPer website, 38%, failed, mostly with compile-time errors) and proposed SaneQL, whose prototype translates to SQL. At VLDB, Jeff Shute and colleagues at Google argued that none of the replacement languages had been successful enough to displace SQL, PRQL included, because adoption means learning a new language and leaving the SQL ecosystem. They added pipe syntax to GoogleSQL instead, shared by F1, BigQuery, Spanner and Procella; BigQuery turned it on for all users in February 2025, and Apache Spark 4.0 shipped its own SQL pipe syntax.

choices.choice: Compile to SQL instead of building an engine
choices.why: Databases already parse, optimise and run SQL well, and most data is reachable through SQL somewhere. Emitting SQL lets a new language work with existing engines, permissions and tools from day one.

choices.choice: Pipelines instead of fixed clause order
choices.why: SQL’s clauses run in an order different from how they are written, and doing anything out of order needs a subquery. A pipeline reads in execution order, and each step can follow any other.
No compiler covers every engine’s functions. PRQL’s s-strings and Malloy’s SQL sources let users drop to the target dialect where the language falls short.
Google’s team concluded that adoption cost, not syntax, kept SQL alternatives niche, so pipe syntax extends SQL backward-compatibly and can be adopted one query at a time.
